## proc_state_array_flat - Proc State Array Flattening {#proc_state_array_flat}


Pass which flattens array elements of the proc state into their constituent
elements. Tuples are flattened in a different pass. Flattening improves
optimizability because each state element can be considered and transformed
in isolation. Flattening also gives the scheduler more flexibility; without
flattening, each element in the aggregate must have the same lifetime.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateArrayFlatteningPass` converts small array-typed `StateElement`s in
a `Proc` into tuple-typed `StateElement`s of their constituent elements,
relying on a subsequent `ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass` to decompose those
tuples into independent state elements.

Breaking array state elements apart allows downstream passes (such as state
narrowing, constant propagation, and dead state elimination) to optimize each
array slot independently, and frees the scheduler from forcing all elements
of the array to share an identical register lifetime.

### How It Works

1. **Flattening Heuristic (`ShouldFlattenStateElement`)**: The pass inspects
   each array-typed `StateElement` owned by the `Proc` and flattens it if its
   array size is at most 2 (`size() <= 2`). (Although `kMaxArrayFlattenSize`
   is defined on the class, the current implementation only flattens arrays
   of length 2 or smaller.)
2. **State Element Conversion (`ArrayToTupleStateTransformer`)**: Using
   `Proc::TransformStateElement`, an array state element of type `T[N]` with
   initial value `[v_0, ..., v_{N-1}]` is replaced by a tuple state element
   of type `(T, ..., T)` with initial value `(v_0, ..., v_{N-1})`:
   * **Transforming `StateRead`s**: Uses of the old array `StateRead` are
     replaced with an `array` node (`<old_state_read>_as_array`) constructed
     from `tuple_index(new_state_read, i)` for `i = 0 .. N-1`.
   * **Transforming `Next` Values**: For each `next_value` targeting the
     state element, its array-typed `value` operand `v` is converted into a
     `tuple` node (`<v>_as_tuple`) whose elements are extracted via
     `array_index(v, indices=[literal(i)])` (using index bit width
     `max(1, CeilOfLog2(N))`).
3. **Cleanup**: The old `next_value` nodes and the original array-typed
   `StateElement` are removed from the `Proc`.

### Example

```
// Before
proc my_proc(s: bits[8][2], init={[0, 1]}) {
  s_read: bits[8][2] = state_read(state_element=s)
  idx0: bits[1] = literal(value=0)
  elem0: bits[8] = array_index(s_read, indices=[idx0])
  next_arr: bits[8][2] = array(elem0, literal(value=2, bits=8))
  next_value(param=s, value=next_arr)
}
```

After `ProcStateArrayFlatteningPass`:

```
// After
proc my_proc(s: (bits[8], bits[8]), init={(0, 1)}) {
  s_read: (bits[8], bits[8]) = state_read(state_element=s)
  e0: bits[8] = tuple_index(s_read, index=0)
  e1: bits[8] = tuple_index(s_read, index=1)
  s_read_as_array: bits[8][2] = array(e0, e1)
  idx0: bits[1] = literal(value=0)
  elem0: bits[8] = array_index(s_read_as_array, indices=[idx0])
  next_arr: bits[8][2] = array(elem0, literal(value=2, bits=8))
  n0: bits[8] = array_index(next_arr, indices=[literal(value=0, bits=1)])
  n1: bits[8] = array_index(next_arr, indices=[literal(value=1, bits=1)])
  next_arr_as_tuple: (bits[8], bits[8]) = tuple(n0, n1)
  next_value(param=s, value=next_arr_as_tuple)
}
```

Subsequent `ArraySimplificationPass`, `TupleSimplificationPass`, and
`ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass` passes then eliminate the intermediate array
and tuple reconstructions and split `s` into two scalar `bits[8]` state
elements.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_array_flattening_pass.h)






## proc_state_bits_shatter - Proc State Bits Shattering {#proc_state_bits_shatter}


Pass which transforms Bits-type elements of the proc state into tuples of
components. Only flattens where it can show that doing so will enable
dynamic state feedback opportunities later (assuming it's followed by a
ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass).

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateBitsShatteringPass` splits wide `bits`-typed `StateElement`s in a
`Proc` into tuples of narrower `bits` components when doing so will expose
independent conditional state updates for `ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass` and
`NextValueOptimizationPass`.

### How It Works

1. **Analyzing `next_value` Nodes for Split Points**: For each `bits`-typed
   `StateElement`, the pass inspects all of its `next_value` nodes:
   * Pass-through updates (`IsNoOpNext`) are ignored because they trivially
     preserve all sub-slices.
   * If any non-no-op `next_value` has a `value` operand that is **not** a
     `concat` node, the state element cannot be split.
   * For each `concat` `next_value`, candidate split boundaries
     (`concat_splits`, ordered from LSB to MSB) are computed from the bit
     widths of the `concat`'s operands (iterated in reverse, since `concat`
     orders operands MSB-to-LSB).
   * Splitting is marked beneficial (`could_benefit_from_splitting = true`)
     if at least one operand of a `concat` is a `priority_sel`, or is a `sel`
     when `options.split_next_value_selects` (default
     `kDefaultSplitNextValueSelects = 4`) is set and
     `sel->cases().size() <= *options.split_next_value_selects`.

2. **Intersecting Split Points**: When multiple non-no-op `next_value` nodes
   update the same state element, their candidate boundary sets are
   intersected (`absl::c_set_intersection`). If
   `could_benefit_from_splitting` is true and the intersection still defines
   more than one component (`split_ends.size() > 1`), the state element is
   shattered.

3. **State Element Transformation (`TuplifyFlatStateElement`)**: Using
   `Proc::TransformStateElement`, the `bits[W]` state element is replaced by
   a tuple `(bits[w_0], bits[w_1], ..., bits[w_{k-1}])` ordered from LSB
   slice to MSB slice:
   * **`initial_value`**: Sliced into a tuple of `Bits` values corresponding
     to `[0, split_ends[0])`, `[split_ends[0], split_ends[1])`, etc.
   * **Transforming `StateRead`s**: Uses of the old `StateRead` are replaced
     with `concat(tuple_index(new_read, k-1), ..., tuple_index(new_read, 0))`
     (reversing the LSB-to-MSB tuple elements to match MSB-to-LSB `concat`
     order).
   * **Transforming `Next` Values**: Each `next_value`'s `value` operand is
     replaced with `tuple(bit_slice(old_val, 0, w_0), ...)`.

### Example

```
// Before
proc my_proc(x: bits[16], init={0}) {
  x_read: bits[16] = state_read(state_element=x)
  x_lo: bits[6] = bit_slice(x_read, start=0, width=6)
  x_mid: bits[1] = bit_slice(x_read, start=6, width=1)
  x_hi: bits[9] = bit_slice(x_read, start=7, width=9)
  cond: bits[1] = or_reduce(x_lo)
  new_mid: bits[1] = priority_sel(cond, cases=[not(x_mid)], default=x_mid)
  next_x: bits[16] = concat(x_hi, new_mid, x_lo)
  next_value(param=x, value=next_x)
}
```

After `ProcStateBitsShatteringPass`:

```
// After
proc my_proc(x: (bits[6], bits[1], bits[9]), init={(0, 0, 0)}) {
  x_read: (bits[6], bits[1], bits[9]) = state_read(state_element=x)
  t_lo: bits[6] = tuple_index(x_read, index=0)
  t_mid: bits[1] = tuple_index(x_read, index=1)
  t_hi: bits[9] = tuple_index(x_read, index=2)
  x_reconstructed: bits[16] = concat(t_hi, t_mid, t_lo)
  // ... next_x computed from x_reconstructed ...
  s_lo: bits[6] = bit_slice(next_x, start=0, width=6)
  s_mid: bits[1] = bit_slice(next_x, start=6, width=1)
  s_hi: bits[9] = bit_slice(next_x, start=7, width=9)
  next_tuple: (bits[6], bits[1], bits[9]) = tuple(s_lo, s_mid, s_hi)
  next_value(param=x, value=next_tuple)
}
```

Followed by `ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass`, `BitSliceSimplificationPass`, and
`NextValueOptimizationPass`, the three components become independent state
elements where only the 1-bit middle element is conditionally updated.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_bits_shattering_pass.h)






## proc_state_elimination - Proc State Elimination {#proc_state_elimination}


Pass which tries to minimize the size and total number of elements of the
proc state by removal of dead state elements and zero-width elements.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateEliminationPass` minimizes the size and total number of state
elements in a `Proc` by removing zero-width, constant, and unobservable
state elements. Fewer state elements directly reduce register count and area
in synthesized hardware.

### How It Works

The pass performs three elimination stages in order:

1. **Removal of Zero-Width State Elements (`RemoveZeroWidthStateElements`)**:
   Any state element whose flat bit count is 0 and whose type contains no
   tokens (`!TypeHasToken`) cannot store information and is removed. Its
   `StateRead` nodes are replaced with literals of its `initial_value`, and
   its `Next` nodes are replaced with empty tuple literals `()` and deleted.

2. **Removal of Constant State Elements (`RemoveConstantStateElements`)**:
   Using a `UnionQueryEngine` combining `StatelessQueryEngine` and a shared
   `LazyTernaryQueryEngine`, the pass checks whether each state element ever
   changes from its `initial_value`. If every `Next` node for a state element
   either passes through one of the state element's own `StateRead`s or
   assigns a value proven equal to `initial_value` (`KnownValue`), the state
   element is constant: all of its `StateRead`s are replaced with
   `Literal(initial_value)`, and its `Next` nodes and state element are
   removed. This step runs in a fixed-point loop to collapse chains of state
   elements whose updates become constant once upstream state elements are
   replaced with literals.

3. **Removal of Unobservable State Elements
   (`RemoveUnobservableStateElements`)**:
   Identifies and removes state elements that cannot affect any observable
   output of the `Proc`:
   * **Single-Cycle State Dependency Analysis**: `StateDependencyVisitor` (a
     `DataflowVisitor<InlineBitmap>`) computes which state elements each node
     depends on within a single activation (unioning both data and control
     sources across `LeafTypeTree` elements).
   * **State-to-State Adjacency Matrix**: For each state element, the pass
     unions the state dependencies of the `value` and `predicate` operands of
     all of its `Next` nodes.
   * **Transitive Observability (`ReachableFrom`)**: Starting from the state
     dependencies of all side-effecting or `invoke` nodes in the `Proc`
     (excluding `state_read`, `next_value`, and `gate`), the pass computes
     the transitive closure over the state-dependency graph.
   * **Elimination**: Any state element not reachable from a side-effecting
     or `invoke` node is unobservable. Its `Next` nodes are removed, any live
     `StateRead`s are replaced with zero-valued literals (`ZeroOfType`), and
     the state element is removed.

### Example

```
// Before
chan out(bits[32], id=0, kind=streaming, ops=send_only,
         flow_control=ready_valid)

top proc my_proc() {
  state_element(const_s, bits[32], init=1)
  state_element(live_s, bits[32], init=0)
  state_element(dead_s, bits[32], init=0)
  c_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=const_s)
  l_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=live_s)
  d_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=dead_s)
  one: bits[32] = literal(value=1)
  next_value(param=const_s, value=one)
  next_value(param=live_s, value=add(l_read, c_read))
  next_value(param=dead_s, value=add(d_read, l_read))
  tkn: token = literal(value=token)
  send.1: token = send(tkn, l_read, channel=out)
}
```

After `ProcStateEliminationPass`:
* `const_s` is replaced by `literal(value=1, bits=32)` because its only
  update writes `1` (matching `init=1`).
* `dead_s` is removed because it only feeds its own `next_value` and never
  influences `send.1` or `live_s`.

```
// After (simplified)
top proc my_proc() {
  state_element(live_s, bits[32], init=0)
  l_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=live_s)
  c_lit: bits[32] = literal(value=1)
  next_value(param=live_s, value=add(l_read, c_lit))
  tkn: token = literal(value=token)
  send.1: token = send(tkn, l_read, channel=out)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_elimination_pass.h)






## proc_state_fsm - Proc State Finite state machine Optimization {#proc_state_fsm}


Pass which tries to minimize the size and total number of elements of the
proc state by optimizing implicit state-machines in the state elements.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateFSMPass` compresses state elements whose values evolve through a
known finite sequence of constants into a compact binary-encoded saturating
counter (state machine).

### How It Works

1. **Query Engine Setup**: Combines `StatelessQueryEngine` and a shared
   `LazyTernaryQueryEngine` via `UnionQueryEngine` to identify `next_value`
   expressions that evaluate to known constants (`IsFullyKnown`).

2. **Detecting Constant Chains (`ConvertConstantChainsToStateMachines`)**:
   In general, `ConstantChainToStateMachine` is designed to compress a shift
   chain of `k` state elements `c[0..k-1]` where `next[c[0]]` is an
   unconditional constant and `next[c[i+1]] == state_read[c[i]]` into a
   single binary counter of width `CeilOfLog2(k) + 1` bits (avoiding a
   `k`-bit one-hot encoding). Currently,
   `ConvertConstantChainsToStateMachines` detects chains of length `k = 1`:
   any state element (of arbitrary width or compound type) that has a single
   unconditional `next_value` (`predicate == std::nullopt`) whose `value` is
   fully known by the query engine.

3. **State Machine Replacement (`ConstantChainToStateMachine`)**:
   * Appends a new state element `state_machine_<names>` of type
     `bits[CeilOfLog2(k) + 1]` initialized to `0` (marked `non_synthesizable`
     if any element in the chain was non-synthesizable).
   * Updates the state machine each tick using a saturating increment:
     `sel(ugt(state, k - 1), cases=[add(state, 1), state])`.
   * Replaces each original `StateRead` at chain index `j` with a `sel`
     indexed by `state_machine` whose `cases` are the reversed initial
     values `[init[j], ..., init[0]]` and whose `default` is the known
     constant `chain_literal`. For `k = 1`, this selects `init[0]` on tick 0
     (when `state_machine == 0`) and `chain_literal` on all subsequent ticks
     (when `state_machine == 1`).
   * Removes the original state elements and their `Next` nodes, and
     repopulates the query engine.

### Example

Suppose a 32-bit state element `s` starts at `0x1234_5678` on the first
activation and unconditionally transitions to `0xDEAD_BEEF` thereafter:

```
// Before
proc my_proc(s: bits[32], init={0x1234_5678}) {
  s_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=s)
  c: bits[32] = literal(value=0xdead_beef)
  next_value(param=s, value=c)
}
```

`ProcStateFSMPass` replaces the 32-bit register `s` with a 1-bit saturating
counter `state_machine_s`:

```
// After
proc my_proc(state_machine_s: bits[1], init={0}) {
  state_machine_s_read: bits[1] = state_read(state_element=state_machine_s)
  one: bits[1] = literal(value=1)
  max: bits[1] = literal(value=0)
  plus_one: bits[1] = add(state_machine_s_read, one)
  too_large: bits[1] = ugt(state_machine_s_read, max)
  next_sm: bits[1] = sel(too_large, cases=[plus_one, state_machine_s_read])
  next_value(param=state_machine_s, value=next_sm)

  init_lit: bits[32] = literal(value=0x1234_5678)
  chain_lit: bits[32] = literal(value=0xdead_beef)
  s_read: bits[32] = sel(state_machine_s_read, cases=[init_lit],
                         default=chain_lit)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_fsm_pass.h)






## proc_state_narrow - Proc State Narrowing {#proc_state_narrow}


Pass which tries to minimize the size of the proc state by narrowing state
elements using range analysis.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateNarrowingPass` reduces the bit width of `bits`-typed
`StateElement`s in a `Proc` by analyzing how state values evolve across ticks
using `ProcStateRangeQueryEngine`. Narrowing state elements directly reduces
the number of flip-flops required in synthesized hardware.

### How It Works

The pass populates a `ProcStateRangeQueryEngine` on the `Proc` (which tracks
both per-bit ternary knowledge and value intervals across proc back-edges)
and inspects each `bits`-typed `StateElement`:

1. **Removing Known Leading Bits (`RemoveLeadingBits` /
   `ProcStateConcatNarrowTransform`)**:
   * Computes the intersection (`ternary_ops::Intersection`) of the ternary
     vectors across all `StateRead` nodes for the state element.
   * Counts the number of leading (most significant) bits whose values are
     known constants (`CountLeadingOnes` on `ToKnownBits`). Note that these
     known leading bits can be any fixed bit pattern (zeros, ones, or a mix).
   * If `known_leading > 0`, the state element is narrowed by slicing off the
     top `known_leading` bits from its `initial_value` and from each
     `next_value` (`bit_slice(next_val, start=0, width=new_width)`). Each
     `StateRead` is reconstructed to the original width via
     `concat(literal(leading_bits), new_state_read)`.

   Example (removing known leading bits):

   ```
   // Before
   proc my_proc(foo: bits[32], init={0}) {
     foo_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=foo)
     low_3: bits[3] = bit_slice(foo_read, start=0, width=3)
     inc: bits[3] = add(low_3, literal(value=1, bits=3))
     next_foo: bits[32] = zero_ext(inc, new_bit_count=32)
     next_value(param=foo, value=next_foo)
   }

   // After
   proc my_proc(foo: bits[3], init={0}) {
     foo_read: bits[3] = state_read(state_element=foo)
     leading_bits_foo: bits[29] = literal(value=0)
     extended_foo: bits[32] = concat(leading_bits_foo, foo_read)
     low_3: bits[3] = bit_slice(extended_foo, start=0, width=3)
     inc: bits[3] = add(low_3, literal(value=1, bits=3))
     next_foo: bits[32] = zero_ext(inc, new_bit_count=32)
     unexpand: bits[3] = bit_slice(next_foo, start=0, width=3)
     next_value(param=foo, value=unexpand)
   }
   ```

2. **Signed Range Narrowing (`RemoveSignBits` /
   `ProcStateSignExtendNarrowTransform`)**:
   * If no leading bits are constant (`known_leading == 0`), the pass queries
     `qe.GetIntervals(state_read)` for each `StateRead` of the state element
     and computes `interval_ops::MinimumSignedBitCount` (taking the maximum
     required signed width `max_signed_bits` across all reads).
   * If `max_signed_bits` is smaller than the state element's bit width, the
     state element is narrowed to `max_signed_bits` bits: its `initial_value`
     and `next_value` operands are truncated with `bit_slice(..., start=0,
     width=max_signed_bits)`, and each `StateRead` is reconstructed to the
     original width via `sign_ext(new_state_read, new_bit_count=old_width)`.

   Example (signed range narrowing for a state element bounded in `[-8, 7]`):

   ```
   // Before
   proc my_proc(bar: bits[32], init={0}) {
     bar_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=bar)
     // ... next_bar proven by ProcStateRangeQueryEngine to stay in [-8, 7]
     next_value(param=bar, value=next_bar)
   }

   // After
   proc my_proc(bar: bits[4], init={0}) {
     bar_read: bits[4] = state_read(state_element=bar)
     extended_bar: bits[32] = sign_ext(bar_read, new_bit_count=32)
     // ... next_bar computed using extended_bar ...
     unexpand: bits[4] = bit_slice(next_bar, start=0, width=4)
     next_value(param=bar, value=unexpand)
   }
   ```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_narrowing_pass.h)






## proc_state_provenance_narrow - Proc State Provenance Narrowing {#proc_state_provenance_narrow}


Pass which tries to minimize the size and total number of elements of the
proc state. This pass works by examining the provenance of the bits making
up the next value to determine which (if any) bits are never actually
modified.

NB This is a separate pass from ProcStateNarrowing for simplicity of
implementation. That pass mostly assumes we'll have a range-analysis which
this does not need.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateProvenanceNarrowingPass` reduces the bit width of `bits`-typed
`StateElement`s in a `Proc` by identifying individual bit positions
(leading, internal, or trailing) that never change from their `initial_value`
across any `next_value` update. Unlike `ProcStateNarrowingPass`, which uses
inter-cycle range analysis to strip leading bits, this pass uses single-cycle
bit provenance and ternary analysis to excise unchanging bit segments at any
offset within the bit vector.

### How It Works

1. **Identifying Unchanged Bits (`UnchangedBits`)**: For each `bits`-typed
   `StateElement` with initial value `initial_bits`, the pass starts with an
   all-ones mask `unchanged_bits` and intersects it across every non-no-op
   `Next` node (`!IsNoOpNext(next)`):
   * **Ternary Match (`LazyTernaryQueryEngine`)**: Computes
     `ternary_known_unchanged`, marking bits in `next->value()` that are
     known constants equal to the corresponding bits in `initial_bits`.
   * **Provenance Match (`BitProvenanceAnalysis`)**: Queries
     `provenance.GetBitSources(next->value())` (`TreeBitSources`) and marks
     any bit range whose source is a `StateRead` of the *same*
     `state_element` at the exact same bit positions
     (`source_bit_index_low == dest_bit_index_low` and
     `source_bit_index_high == dest_bit_index_high`).
   * A bit remains set in `unchanged_bits` if, for every `Next` node, it is
     preserved via either provenance or ternary equivalence.

2. **Extracting Bit Segments (`ExtractBitSegments`)**: If `unchanged_bits`
   is non-zero, the state element's bit range is partitioned into contiguous
   `BitSegment`s ordered from MSB to LSB. Each segment is either a constant
   segment (holding the corresponding slice of `initial_bits`) or a variable
   segment (`value == std::nullopt`).

3. **State Element Transformation (`NarrowTransform`)**: Using
   `Proc::TransformStateElement`, the state element is narrowed to the
   concatenation of its variable segments (`NarrowValue`):
   * **Transforming `StateRead`s**: Reconstructs the original width by
     concatenating (from MSB to LSB) `Literal` nodes for constant segments
     and `BitSlice` nodes (or `new_state_read` directly if there is only a
     single variable segment) for variable segments.
   * **Transforming `Next` Values**: Slices only the variable segments from
     `old_next->value()` (`BitSlice`) and concatenates them to form the
     narrowed `next_value`.

### Example

Consider a 96-bit state element `foo` whose middle 32 bits (`[32:64]`) are
initialized to `0xFFFF_0000` and are always either copied from `foo` or
overwritten with `0xFFFF_0000`:

```
// Before
proc my_proc(foo: bits[96], init={0x0000_0000_ffff_0000_0000_0000}) {
  foo_read: bits[96] = state_read(state_element=foo)
  lo: bits[32] = add(bit_slice(foo_read, start=0, width=32),
                     literal(value=1, bits=32))
  mid: bits[32] = bit_slice(foo_read, start=32, width=32)
  hi: bits[32] = add(bit_slice(foo_read, start=64, width=32),
                     literal(value=2, bits=32))
  next_foo: bits[96] = concat(hi, mid, lo)
  next_value(param=foo, value=next_foo)
}
```

`ProcStateProvenanceNarrowingPass` removes the unchanging middle 32 bits,
narrowing `foo` from 96 bits to 64 bits:

```
// After
proc my_proc(foo: bits[64], init={0x0000_0000_0000_0000}) {
  foo_read: bits[64] = state_read(state_element=foo)
  var_hi: bits[32] = bit_slice(foo_read, start=32, width=32)
  const_mid: bits[32] = literal(value=0xffff_0000)
  var_lo: bits[32] = bit_slice(foo_read, start=0, width=32)
  foo_reconstructed: bits[96] = concat(var_hi, const_mid, var_lo)
  // ... next_foo computed from foo_reconstructed ...
  next_hi: bits[32] = bit_slice(next_foo, start=64, width=32)
  next_lo: bits[32] = bit_slice(next_foo, start=0, width=32)
  next_foo_slice_reduced: bits[64] = concat(next_hi, next_lo)
  next_value(param=foo, value=next_foo_slice_reduced)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_provenance_narrowing_pass.h)






## proc_state_tuple_flat - Proc State Tuple Flattening {#proc_state_tuple_flat}


Pass which flattens tuple elements of the proc state into their constituent
components. Array elements are flattened in a different pass. Flattening
improves optimizability because each state element can be considered and
transformed in isolation. Flattening also gives the scheduler more
flexibility; without flattening, each element in the aggregate must have the
same lifetime.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass` recursively decomposes tuple-typed
`StateElement`s in a `Proc` into separate leaf (non-tuple) `StateElement`s.
(Array-typed state elements are not decomposed by this pass; small arrays are
first converted into tuples by `ProcStateArrayFlatteningPass`.)

### How It Works

If a `Proc` has at least one tuple-typed `StateElement`
(`HasTupleStateElement`), `FlattenState` rebuilds the proc state:

1. **Decomposing Initial Values (`DecomposeValue`)**: Each state element's
   `initial_value` is recursively flattened across nested tuples into a list
   of `num_components` leaf `Value`s.
   * If `num_components == 1` (e.g., a scalar state element or a 1-element
     tuple), the new state element retains the original name.
   * If `num_components > 1`, each leaf state element is named
     `<name>_0`, `<name>_1`, etc.
   * If `num_components == 0` (an empty tuple `()`), the state element
     decomposes into zero components and is eliminated.

2. **Decomposing `StateRead`s (`ComposeNode`)**: For each `StateRead` of an
   original state element, a `StateRead` (preserving `predicate` and `label`)
   is created on each corresponding leaf state element. The original tuple
   structure is reconstructed from the leaf `StateRead`s using `Tuple` nodes
   and replaces all uses of the original `StateRead`.

3. **Decomposing `Next` Values (`DecomposeNode`)**: For each `Next` node of
   an original state element, `next->value()` is recursively decomposed into
   leaf nodes by inserting `TupleIndex` operations. A separate `Next` node
   (preserving `predicate` and `label`) is created for each leaf state
   element.

4. **Replacing Proc State (`ReplaceProcState`)**: All old `Next` nodes and
   state elements are removed and replaced with the flattened leaf
   `StateElement`s, `StateRead`s, and `Next` nodes.

### Example

```
// Before
proc my_proc(s: (bits[8], (bits[16], bits[32])), init={(1, (2, 3))}) {
  s_read: (bits[8], (bits[16], bits[32])) = state_read(state_element=s)
  a: bits[8] = tuple_index(s_read, index=0)
  inner: (bits[16], bits[32]) = tuple_index(s_read, index=1)
  next_s: (bits[8], (bits[16], bits[32])) = tuple(a, inner)
  next_value(param=s, value=next_s)
}
```

After `ProcStateTupleFlatteningPass`:

```
// After
proc my_proc(s_0: bits[8], s_1: bits[16], s_2: bits[32], init={1, 2, 3}) {
  s_0_read: bits[8] = state_read(state_element=s_0)
  s_1_read: bits[16] = state_read(state_element=s_1)
  s_2_read: bits[32] = state_read(state_element=s_2)
  reconstructed_inner: (bits[16], bits[32]) = tuple(s_1_read, s_2_read)
  s_read: (bits[8], (bits[16], bits[32])) = tuple(s_0_read,
                                                  reconstructed_inner)
  a: bits[8] = tuple_index(s_read, index=0)
  inner: (bits[16], bits[32]) = tuple_index(s_read, index=1)
  next_s: (bits[8], (bits[16], bits[32])) = tuple(a, inner)
  next_0: bits[8] = tuple_index(next_s, index=0)
  next_inner: (bits[16], bits[32]) = tuple_index(next_s, index=1)
  next_1: bits[16] = tuple_index(next_inner, index=0)
  next_2: bits[32] = tuple_index(next_inner, index=1)
  next_value(param=s_0, value=next_0)
  next_value(param=s_1, value=next_1)
  next_value(param=s_2, value=next_2)
}
```

Subsequent `TupleSimplificationPass` and `DeadCodeEliminationPass` runs
simplify away the intermediate `tuple` and `tuple_index` nodes.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/proc_state_tuple_flattening_pass.h)






## ram_rewrite - RAM Rewrite {#ram_rewrite}


Pass that rewrites RAMs of one type to a new type. Generally this will be
some kind of lowering from more abstract to concrete RAMs.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `RamRewritePass` facilitates the transformation of RAM (Random Access
Memory) interfaces within an XLS package. Its primary role is to lower more
abstract RAM models to concrete RAM types that are directly implementable by
target hardware. This is a crucial step in the hardware generation flow.

The pass is driven by `RamRewrite` configurations, which specify the original
RAM type (`from_config`), the target RAM type (`to_config`), and the mapping
between logical channel names (e.g., `read_req`) and their corresponding
physical channel names in the IR.

Key aspects of the `RamRewritePass` include:

1.  **RAM Abstraction Levels**:
    *   **`kAbstract`**: A high-level, generic RAM model that provides a
        simplified interface.
    *   **`k1RW` (One Read/Write Port)**: A concrete RAM with a single port
        that can perform either a read or a write operation per cycle. Its
        request channel typically includes address, data, write enable, and
        read enable signals bundled together.
    *   **`k1R1W` (One Read, One Write Port)**: A concrete RAM with separate,
        independent read and write ports, enabling simultaneous read and
        write operations.

2.  **Channel Rewiring and Repacking**:
    The core function of the pass is to replace existing `send` and `receive`
    operations associated with the `from_config` RAM channels with new `send`
    and `receive` operations connected to the `to_config` RAM channels. This
    often necessitates "repacking" the data payloads to match the new channel
    types.

    *   **Repacking for `send` operations**: The `RepackPayload` function
        transforms the structure of an old `send` operation's operand to
        match the expected input format of the new RAM channel. This can
        involve adding literal values (e.g., `write_enable` or `read_enable`
        bits for `k1RW` RAMs), dropping unused fields, or simply passing
        through data if the formats are compatible.

        Example (Abstract Read Request to 1RW Request):
        An abstract read request might be a tuple `(address, mask)`. When
        rewritten to a `k1RW` RAM, its request channel expects `(address,
        data, write_mask, read_mask, write_enable, read_enable)`. The pass
        will construct a new tuple, filling `data`, `write_mask` with zero
        literals, setting `write_enable` to `0b0` and `read_enable` to `0b1`.

        ```
        // Original abstract read request send
        send_abstract_read_req: token = send(tok,
                                             (addr, mask),
                                             channel=abstract_read_req)

        // Transformed 1RW request send (simplified)
        send_1rw_req: token =
                      send(tok,
                           (addr, data, wmask, mask, we, re),
                           channel=1rw_req)
        ```


    *   **Repacking for `receive` operations**: Similarly, the output of the
        new `receive` operation (which adheres to the `to_config` channel
        type) is repacked to conform to the expected output format of the
        original `from_config` channel. This ensures that downstream logic
        that consumes the received data continues to function correctly.

3.  **Channel Creation and Removal**: The pass dynamically creates new
    channels that correspond to the `to_config` RAM type and subsequently
    removes the original channels associated with the `from_config` RAM type.
    This ensures a clean transition to the new RAM interface.

4.  **Proc-Scoped Channels**: The pass properly handles both global and
    proc-scoped channels. If a `proc_name` is specified in the `RamRewrite`
    configuration, the channels are treated as local to that particular proc.

5.  **Error Handling**: The pass includes robust checks for potential issues
    such as type mismatches (e.g., inconsistencies in address width between
    `from_config` and `to_config`) and unsupported transformation scenarios,
    returning informative errors where applicable.

This pass is a critical element in the XLS compilation flow, enabling the
compiler to generate optimized hardware for diverse RAM architectures while
preserving the functional correctness of the original design.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/ram_rewrite_pass.h)






## reassociation - Reassociation {#reassociation}


Reassociates associative operations to reduce delay by transforming chains of
operations to a balanced tree of operations, and gathering together constants
in the expression for folding.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `ReassociationPass` is an optimization pass in XLS that reorders
associative operations such as addition (`add`), subtraction (`sub`), and
signed/unsigned multiplication (`smul`, `umul`). Its primary objectives are
to reduce the critical path delay of the synthesized hardware and to
facilitate further constant folding by grouping literal operands.

This pass is crucial for transforming deep, unbalanced chains of operations
(e.g., `(((A + B) + C) + D)`) into more balanced tree structures
(e.g., `((A + B) + (C + D))`). It also effectively gathers together constant
operands within an associative expression, making them amenable to subsequent
constant folding optimizations.

**Key Concepts**:

*   **Associativity**: The pass exploits the associative property of
    operations like addition and multiplication. This property states that
    for an associative operation `op`, `(A op B) op C` is mathematically
    equivalent to `A op (B op C)`. Reassociation leverages this to
    restructure the computation graph.
*   **Critical Path Delay Reduction**: A deep, unbalanced chain of operations
    in the IR directly translates to a long critical path in the hardware,
    which limits the maximum clock frequency. By rebalancing these chains
    into a shallower tree, the pass effectively reduces the overall critical
    path delay.
*   **Constant Folding Facilitation**: Grouping constant operands together
    within an associative expression allows the `ConstantFoldingPass` to
    combine them into a single literal. This simplifies the expression and
    reduces dynamic computation.
*   **Overflow Handling**: The pass is designed to carefully consider
    potential overflow conditions, particularly for signed arithmetic and
    operations involving different bit widths. This ensures that the semantic
    correctness of the original computation is rigorously preserved during
    reassociation.

**How it Works**:

1.  **`AssociativeElements` Class**: This internal helper class is central
    to the pass's operation. For each node identified as part of an
    associative chain, it recursively collects and models:
    *   `variables_`: Non-constant leaf nodes (e.g., parameters or results of
        other complex expressions).
    *   `constants_`: Constant leaf nodes (i.e., `literal` operations).
    *   `op_`: The primary associative operation (`Op::kAdd`, `Op::kSMul`,
        etc.) governing the combination of these elements.
    *   `needs_negate`: A boolean flag indicating if a variable needs to be
        logically negated, typically arising from subtraction operations
        (e.g., `A - B` is conceptually treated as `A + (-B)`).
    *   `overflows_`: A flag indicating whether the sub-expression
        represented by this `AssociativeElements` object can potentially
        overflow at its current bit-width. This information is crucial for
        safe combination.
    *   `depth_`: Tracks the depth of the longest chain of associative
        operations leading to this particular node.

2.  **`OneShotReassociationVisitor`**: This visitor traverses the IR in a
    single pass to compute and collect the `AssociativeElements` for each
    relevant node. It includes logic to handle various operations:
    *   **Associative Operations (`Add`, `Sub`, `SMul`, `UMul`)**: For these
        operations, it recursively combines the `AssociativeElements` of its
        operands, managing negation for subtraction and tracking potential
        overflow conditions.
    *   **`Neg`**: Handles negation by logically flipping the `needs_negate`
        flag of its operand's `AssociativeElements` representation.
    *   **Extensions (`ZeroExtend`, `SignExtend`) and `Concat` operations
        that effectively act as `ZeroExtend`**: These operations can widen a
        value without fundamentally changing its underlying numerical value.
        The pass attempts to "see through" these by propagating the
        `AssociativeElements` of the inner operand if no overflow occurs and
        signedness compatibility is maintained.

3.  **`ReassociationCache`**: This caching mechanism stores the computed
    `AssociativeElements` for each node. This avoids redundant computations
    during iterative passes and helps ensure that analyses are kept
    up-to-date even after transformations have altered the graph structure.

4.  **`Reassociate` Function (Main Loop)**:
    *   **Fixed-Point Iteration**: The pass operates in a fixed-point manner.
        It identifies nodes that are prime candidates for reassociation and
        repeatedly applies the transformation until no further beneficial
        changes can be made across the entire function.
    *   **Candidate Selection**: Nodes are selected for reassociation if they
        meet specific criteria, including:
        *   Not already a leaf node (i.e., they are part of a larger
            associative chain).
        *   Not composed entirely of constants (these are handled by the
            separate `ConstantFoldingPass`).
        *   Having users that require materialization (i.e., the
            reassociation is not trivially hidden by other optimizations).
        *   Their current depth in the IR graph is greater than the minimum
            possible depth for a balanced tree of its elements, or they
            contain multiple constants that can be meaningfully grouped.
    *   **`ReassociateOneOperation`**: This function is responsible for
        actually reconstructing the selected associative operation into a
        balanced tree:
        *   **Grouping Constants**: It first groups all constant operands
            together to be combined by `ConstantFoldingPass`.
        *   **Balancing Tree**: It then constructs a balanced binary tree
            using the variable elements, minimizing the depth of the overall
            computation.  The tree is typically biased to the left to ensure
            a consistent output structure, which can further aid subsequent
            Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE).
        *   **Negation and Extension Handling**: It correctly applies
            necessary negations and extensions (sign-extend/zero-extend)
            during the reconstruction process to strictly preserve semantic
            equivalence.

**Benefits**:

*   **Reduced Critical Path**: By transforming deep chains of operations into
    balanced trees, the pass significantly reduces the critical path delay in
    the generated hardware, allowing for higher clock frequencies.
*   **Improved Constant Folding**: Grouping constant operands together within
    associative expressions enables `ConstantFoldingPass` to reduce them to
    single literals, thereby simplifying the IR and reducing dynamic
    computation.
*   **Enhanced IR Structure**: Creates a more canonical and optimized
    structure for associative expressions, which can benefit subsequent
    optimization passes by providing a clearer and more efficient
    representation of the computation.

Example (Rebalancing additions):
Consider a deep, left-leaning chain of addition operations:


```
// Original IR snippet (deep left-leaning chain)
fn deep_add(a: bits[32], b: bits[32], c: bits[32], d: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  add.1: bits[32] = add(a, b)
  add.2: bits[32] = add(add.1, c)
  ret add.3: bits[32] = add(add.2, d)
}
```


The `ReassociationPass` would transform this into a balanced tree structure:


```
// Optimized IR (after ReassociationPass and a subsequent DCE pass)
fn deep_add(a: bits[32], b: bits[32], c: bits[32], d: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  add.left: bits[32] = add(a, b)
  add.right: bits[32] = add(c, d)
  ret add.final: bits[32] = add(add.left, add.right)
}
```

This transformation reduces the maximum depth of the additions from 3 to 2,
directly improving potential timing performance.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/reassociation_pass.h)






## recv_default - Receive default value simplification {#recv_default}


Optimization which removes useless selects between the data value of a
conditional or non-blocking receive and the default value of the receive (all
zeros).

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `ReceiveDefaultValueSimplificationPass` is a proc-level optimization pass
(`OptimizationProcPass`) that identifies and eliminates redundant binary
`select` and `priority_select` operations choosing between the data output of
a conditional or non-blocking `receive` and an all-zeros value.

In XLS, when a conditional `receive` has a false predicate, or when a
non-blocking `receive` has no data available (its valid bit is `0`), its data
output (`tuple_index(receive_node, index=1)`) is already defined to be all
zeros. Frontends or earlier passes often emit an explicit `select` or
`priority_select` that forces the value to zero under those same conditions.

**How it Works**:

Using `StatelessQueryEngine`, the pass walks the proc in topological order
and inspects each two-way `Select` (`cases=[on_false, on_true]`, no default)
and single-case `PrioritySelect` (`cases=[on_true], default=on_false`). It
matches `MatchUselessSelectAfterReceive` when:

1.  `on_true` is `tuple_index(receive, index=1)` (the data payload of a
    `Receive` node).
2.  `on_false` is known to be all zeros
    (`KnownValue(on_false)->IsAllZeros()`).
3.  One of the following selector conditions holds:
    *   **Conditional `receive`**: `receive` is predicated and its predicate
        is `selector`.
    *   **Non-blocking `receive`**: `receive` is non-blocking and `selector`
        is the valid bit (`tuple_index(..., index=2)`) of a non-blocking
        `receive`.

When matched, the pass replaces the `select` or `priority_select` directly
with `on_true` (`tuple_index(receive, index=1)`).

Example (Conditional `receive` with redundant `select`):

```
// Original IR snippet
chan in(bits[32], kind=streaming, ops=receive_only, flow_control=ready_valid)

proc p(pred: bits[1], s: bits[32], init={1, 42}) {
  tkn: token = literal(value=token)
  // Data is already 0 if pred is 0
  receive.1: (token, bits[32]) = receive(tkn, predicate=pred, channel=in)
  receive_data: bits[32] = tuple_index(receive.1, index=1)
  zero: bits[32] = literal(value=0)
  select.2: bits[32] = sel(pred, cases=[zero, receive_data])
  next (pred, select.2)
}

// Optimized IR snippet
chan in(bits[32], kind=streaming, ops=receive_only, flow_control=ready_valid)

proc p(pred: bits[1], s: bits[32], init={1, 42}) {
  tkn: token = literal(value=token)
  receive.1: (token, bits[32]) = receive(tkn, predicate=pred, channel=in)
  receive_data: bits[32] = tuple_index(receive.1, index=1)
  next (pred, receive_data)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/receive_default_value_simplification_pass.h)






## repopulate_cached_proc_state_info - Recompute and repopulate the cached proc-state element information. {#repopulate_cached_proc_state_info}


Fully populates the cached proc-state information in the query engines.

This repopulates the givens in PartialInfoQueryEngine and
LazyTernaryQueryEngine.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

`RepopulateCachedProcStateInfoPass` (`repopulate_cached_proc_state_info`) is
an analysis-refresh pass for `Proc`s that recomputes inductive proc-state
invariants and updates the shared query engines cached in
`OptimizationContext`. It does not directly mutate the IR (always returning
`false`), but enables stronger downstream simplifications in passes that rely
on cached state-element facts.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Inductive State Range Analysis**:
    The pass populates a `ProcStateRangeQueryEngine` (`base_qe`) on the
    target `Proc`. This analysis examines the initial values and `next_value`
    transitions of the proc's state elements to prove inductive value ranges
    and known-bit invariants on `state_read` nodes across all proc ticks.

2.  **Updating Cached Query Engines**:
    Using `CachedStateElementQueryEngine::FromContext`, the pass retrieves
    the shared `PartialInfoQueryEngine` and `LazyTernaryQueryEngine`
    instances for the `Proc` from `OptimizationContext` and invokes
    `ComputeWithStateInfo(base_qe)` on each. This injects the newly proven
    state-element intervals and ternary bits as "givens" into those cached
    engines so subsequent passes (such as `SelectSimplificationPass`,
    `SelectRangeSimplificationPass`, and `NarrowingPass`) can exploit them
    without rerunning `ProcStateRangeQueryEngine`.

Example (Enabling downstream simplification via cached state ranges):

```
// Proc whose state `cnt` starts at 0 and wraps within [0, 3]:
proc counter(cnt: bits[8], init={0}) {
  one: bits[8] = literal(value=1)
  inc: bits[8] = add(cnt, one)
  three: bits[8] = literal(value=3)
  wrap: bits[1] = ugt(cnt, three)
  zero: bits[8] = literal(value=0)
  next_cnt: bits[8] = sel(wrap, cases=[inc, zero])
  next (next_cnt)
}

// After RepopulateCachedProcStateInfoPass populates the cached
// PartialInfoQueryEngine and LazyTernaryQueryEngine with the invariant
// cnt in [0, 3] (upper 6 bits known 0), downstream passes can fold `wrap`
// to 0 and narrow `cnt`.
```

## resource_sharing - Resource Sharing {#resource_sharing}


!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `ResourceSharingPass` is a critical optimization pass in XLS that aims to
reduce hardware area by sharing common computational resources (e.g., adders,
multipliers) among different parts of the design. This is achieved by
identifying mutually exclusive operations—operations that are guaranteed not
to execute at the same time—and then transforming the IR to allow them to
share the same physical hardware resource through multiplexing.

The pass is configured with a `ProfitabilityGuard` enum, which determines the
heuristic used to select which sharing opportunities to exploit:

*   **`kInDegree`**: Prioritizes sharing based on the in-degree of nodes in
    a conceptual "folding graph." This heuristic favors nodes that are
    potential "destinations" for folding, especially those with more distinct
    "source" operations that can be multiplexed into them. This approach is
    often effective for asymmetric folding scenarios where one complex
    operation can subsume several simpler ones.
*   **`kCliques`**: Selects sharing opportunities based on identifying
    cliques (groups of mutually exclusive operations) in the folding graph.
    This approach is particularly suitable for symmetric folding scenarios
    where multiple operations of similar complexity can all share a single
    resource.
*   **`kRandom`**: Randomly selects a subset of potential folding actions.
    This is typically used for testing, fuzzing, or exploration purposes
    rather than for deterministic optimization.
*   **`kAlways`**: Attempts to perform all possible resource sharing that is
    identified as legal. This is generally used for aggressive optimization
    benchmarking or during specific testing phases.

The core mechanism of `ResourceSharingPass` involves several stages:

1.  **Mutual Exclusion Analysis**:
    *   **`ComputeMutualExclusionAnalysis`**: This is a central function that
        identifies pairs or groups of operations that are mutually exclusive.
        It builds a "mutual exclusivity relation" between nodes, proving that
        two operations are guaranteed not to be active simultaneously.
    *   It leverages `NodeForwardDependencyAnalysis` to trace dataflow
        dependencies and `BddQueryEngine` (Binary Decision Diagrams) for
        precise logical analysis. The `BddQueryEngine` is critical for
        proving that a particular operation's value does not influence
        another under specific conditions (e.g., when a particular arm of a
        `select` operation is chosen).
    *   The analysis primarily focuses on `PrioritySelect` operations, as
        these explicitly define conditional execution paths, which naturally
        create clear mutual exclusivity between their cases. The analysis is
        conservative and avoids making assumptions through `Invoke` nodes
        before function inlining to ensure correctness.

2.  **Folding Graph Construction**: Based on the results of the mutual
    exclusivity analysis, a `FoldingGraph` is constructed. This graph
    represents potential "folding actions," where a "source" operation can be
    "folded" into a "destination" operation, implying that they can share the
    same underlying hardware resource. This sharing is controlled by a
    `select` operation whose condition is derived from the mutual exclusivity
    proof.

3.  **Profitability Estimation**:
    *   The pass utilizes `AreaEstimator` and `DelayEstimator` tools to
        assess the profitability of each potential folding action. This
        involves a cost-benefit analysis.
    *   `EstimateAreaForSelectingASingleInput`: Calculates the area overhead
        associated with adding multiplexers (`select` logic) required to
        steer the inputs to a shared resource.
    *   `EstimateAreaForNegatingNode`: Estimates the area cost if an operand
        needs to be negated (e.g., when folding a `sub` operation into an
        `add` operation that operates on the negated operand).
    *   The `area_saved` for a folding action is calculated as the estimated
        area of the "from" node minus the area overhead of the multiplexers
        and any additional required logic.
    *   `DelayAnalysis` is used to consider the impact of sharing on the
        critical path delay. The `kMaxDelaySpread` constant defines an
        acceptable limit for the increase in delay due to multiplexing.

4.  **Selection of Folding Actions**:
    *   `SelectFoldingActions`: This function, guided by the chosen
        `ProfitabilityGuard` heuristic, selects a subset of the legal and
        profitable folding actions to perform.
    *   It prioritizes actions that offer significant area savings while
        keeping delay impacts within acceptable bounds.
    *   The selected actions are sorted (e.g., by descending area savings)
        and then "legalized" (`LegalizeSequenceOfFolding`) to prevent
        overlapping or conflicting transformations from being applied.

5.  **IR Transformation**: Once a final set of `NaryFoldingAction`s is
    selected, the IR is transformed to implement the sharing. This involves:
    *   Creating new `select` or `priority_select` operations (or chains of
        them) to multiplex the inputs of the shared resource based on the
        conditions derived from the original mutual exclusivity.
    *   Replacing the original "from" operations with the output of the newly
        created multiplexing structure, which then feeds into the "to"
        (shared) operation.
    *   Removing the now redundant "from" operations.

Example:
Consider two `umul` operations, `mul0(a, b)` and `mul1(c, d)`, which are
mutually exclusive (e.g., they are in different arms of a `priority_select`).
The `ResourceSharingPass` might identify this and transform the IR to use a
single shared `umul` hardware resource:


```
// Original IR snippet (simplified)
selector: bits[1] = ...
mul0: bits[32] = umul(a, b, width=32)
mul1: bits[32] = umul(c, d, width=32)
ret result: bits[32] = priority_sel(selector, cases=[mul0], default=mul1)
```


After `ResourceSharingPass` (conceptual representation, as actual IR is more
complex with explicit multiplexing):


```
// Optimized IR snippet (simplified)
selector: bits[1] = ...

// Multiplexed inputs to the shared multiplier
input_a_mux: bits[32] = priority_sel(selector, cases=[a], default=c)
input_b_mux: bits[32] = priority_sel(selector, cases=[b], default=d)

// Shared multiplier operation
umul_shared: bits[32] = umul(input_a_mux, input_b_mux, width=32)

ret result: bits[32] = umul_shared // The shared multiplier is now the result
```

This pass is vital for achieving high-quality hardware designs by efficiently
utilizing available hardware resources, particularly in designs with
significant conditional logic.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/resource_sharing_pass.h)

## select_lifting - Select Lifting {#select_lifting}


Pass which replace the pattern
  v = sel (c, array[i], array[j], ...)
where all cases of the select reference the same array, to the code
  z = sel (c, i, j, ...)
  v = array[z]

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `SelectLiftingPass` is an optimization pass in XLS that restructures
`select` and `priority_select` operations to improve hardware efficiency.
It identifies scenarios where a `select`'s cases are all derived from a
common "shared" operation (such as an `array_index` or a binary arithmetic
operation) and "lifts" that shared operation out of the `select`. This
transformation effectively moves the multiplexing (the `select`) from the
*output* of the shared operation to its *input*, which often leads to
significant hardware savings and can sometimes improve performance.

This pass is particularly effective in two main scenarios:

1.  **Lifting `ArrayIndex` Operations**:
    When all cases of a `select` are `array_index` operations on the *same
    array*, the pass can lift the `array_index` out of the `select`. It
    creates a new `select` that chooses between the *indices* of the original
    `array_index` operations. The result of this new `select` (the chosen
    index) is then used in a single, shared `array_index` operation. This
    replaces multiple array reads followed by a wide data multiplexer with a
    smaller index multiplexer followed by a single array read, which is
    generally much more area-efficient.


    ```
    // Original IR snippet
    v = sel(c, array[i], array[j])

    // Optimized IR (after lifting)
    z = sel(c, i, j)
    v = array[z]
    ```


2.  **Lifting Binary Operations**:
    When all cases of a `select` are binary operations of the same kind
    (e.g., all `add`s, `sub`s, or `mul`s) and share one common operand, the
    binary operation can be lifted out of the `select`. A new `select` is
    created to choose between the "other" (non-shared) operands. The result
    of this new `select` is then used in a single, shared binary operation
    with the common operand.


    ```
    // Original IR snippet
    v = sel(c, x + a, x + b)

    // Optimized IR (after lifting)
    z = sel(c, a, b)
    v = x + z
    ```


**Profitability and Applicability Guards**:

The pass includes several "guards" to ensure that the transformation is both
applicable and profitable:

*   **`CanLiftSelect`**: This function checks if a `select` is a candidate
    for lifting. For `ArrayIndex` lifting, it verifies that all cases are
    indeed `array_index` operations on the same array and that their index
    types are compatible. For binary operation lifting, it identifies a
    common `shared_node` across all cases and ensures the operation type is
    consistent and supported (e.g., `add`, `sub`, `and`, `or`, `mul`,
    shifts). It also handles "identity" cases, where one of the `select`'s
    cases is the shared operand itself.

*   **`ShouldLiftSelect`**: This function determines if a liftable `select`
    should actually be transformed, based on profitability heuristics:
    *   **Area Estimation**: For binary operations, it performs a simple
        cost-benefit analysis based on the bit-widths of the original and
        transformed operations. The transformation is generally considered
        profitable if the total bit-width of the new, narrower `select` and
        the shared operation is less than or equal to the total bit-width of
        the original `select` and all the individual binary operations (if
        they were single-use).
    *   **Delay Estimation**: If a `delay_model` is provided, the pass uses
        `CriticalPathDelayAnalysis` to estimate the impact of the
        transformation on the critical path. Lifting is avoided if it is
        predicted to increase the latency. This is particularly important for
        scenarios like converting multiple constant-shifts into a single
        variable-shift, which is often more expensive in hardware.
    *   **Heuristics for High-Latency Operations**: For high-latency
        operations like multiplication, lifting is more cautiously applied,
        especially if it involves identity cases, to avoid potentially
        degrading performance.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Worklist-based Iteration**: The pass maintains a worklist of `select`
    and `priority_select` nodes that are candidates for optimization. It
    iterates through this worklist, applying transformations until no more
    profitable lifting opportunities can be found.

2.  **Applicability and Profitability Checks**: For each `select` in the
    worklist, it calls `CanLiftSelect` and then `ShouldLiftSelect` to
    determine if a valid and beneficial transformation exists.

3.  **IR Transformation**: If a transformation is approved:
    *   **`LiftSelectForArrayIndex`**: Rewires the IR for `array_index`
        lifting by creating a new `select` for the indices and a new shared
        `array_index`.
    *   **`LiftSelectForBinaryOperation`**: Rewires the IR for binary
        operation lifting by creating a new `select` for the non-shared
        operands and a new shared binary operation. It correctly handles
        identity cases by inserting the appropriate identity literal (e.g.,
        `0` for `add`, `-1` for `and`) into the new `select`.

4.  **Cleanup**: The original `select` node, now redundant, is marked for
    deletion, which is typically handled by a subsequent
    `DeadCodeEliminationPass`. Any new `select` nodes created during the
    transformation are added to the worklist, allowing for potential further
    optimizations.

By systematically applying these transformations, `SelectLiftingPass` plays a
crucial role in optimizing multiplexer-heavy designs, leading to more
efficient use of hardware resources and improved overall performance.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/select_lifting_pass.h)






## select_merge - Select Merging {#select_merge}


!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `SelectMergingPass` merges consecutive `OneHotSelect` or `PrioritySelect`
operations in a `FunctionBase` into a single, larger select operation of the
same kind. Flattening cascades of single-use selects into a unified select
simplifies the IR and allows downstream passes (such as select
simplification) and hardware synthesis tools to optimize across all cases at
once.

**How it Works**:

The pass traverses the IR in topological order (`TopoSort`) and invokes
`MergeSelectNode` on each `OneHotSelect` and `PrioritySelect` node:

1.  **Merging `OneHotSelect` Operations**:
    *   **Pattern**: An outer `OneHotSelect` where one or more cases are
        themselves single-use `OneHotSelect` nodes (`users().size() == 1`).
    *   **Transformation**: Constructs a single merged `OneHotSelect`:
        *   Contiguous runs of unmerged cases have their corresponding
            selector slice extracted via `bit_slice`.
        *   For each case `i` that is a single-use `OneHotSelect`, bit `i` of
            the outer selector is extracted (`bit_slice`), sign-extended to
            the bit-width of the inner selector (`sign_ext`), and bitwise
            `and`-ed with the inner selector. Its cases are spliced directly
            into the merged case list.
        *   All selector pieces are concatenated (from MSB to LSB) via
            `CreateFlattenedConcat` (so nested `Concat` trees in selector
            pieces are flattened immediately) to form the new selector.

2.  **Merging `PrioritySelect` Operations**:
    *   **Selector Inversion for 1-Bit `PrioritySelect`s**: If a 1-bit
        `PrioritySelect` has a single-use `PrioritySelect` as `cases[0]` and
        its `default_value` is *not* a single-use `PrioritySelect`, the pass
        first negates the 1-bit selector (`not`) and swaps `cases[0]` with
        `default_value`. Merging an inner `PrioritySelect` from the
        `default_value` position is simpler because its default value
        directly becomes the merged `default_value` without needing an
        explicit `inner_selector == 0` fallback condition.
    *   **Case Merging**: For any case `i` that is a single-use
        `PrioritySelect`, bit `i` of the outer selector is sign-extended and
        `and`-ed with the inner selector to guard the inner cases, followed
        by an additional case for the inner `default_value` guarded by
        `and(outer_selector[i], eq(inner_selector, 0))`.
    *   **Default Value Merging**: If the outer `default_value` is a
        single-use `PrioritySelect`, its selector and cases are appended at
        the lowest-priority end of the merged `PrioritySelect`, and its
        `default_value` becomes the new outer `default_value`.
    *   All selector pieces are concatenated via `CreateFlattenedConcat` to
        form the merged selector.

**Key Conditions for Merging**:

*   **Single Use**: An inner select is only merged if `users().size() == 1`,
    preventing logic duplication.
*   **Matching Select Types**: `OneHotSelect` nodes are only merged into
    `OneHotSelect`, and `PrioritySelect` nodes are only merged into
    `PrioritySelect`.

Example (`OneHotSelect` merging):

```
// Original IR snippet
fn f(p0: bits[2], p1: bits[2], x: bits[32], y: bits[32],
     z: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  one_hot_sel.1: bits[32] = one_hot_sel(p0, cases=[x, y])
  ret one_hot_sel.2: bits[32] = one_hot_sel(p1, cases=[one_hot_sel.1, z])
}
```

Because `one_hot_sel.1` has only one user (`one_hot_sel.2`),
`SelectMergingPass` merges them into a single 3-case `one_hot_sel`:

```
// Optimized IR
fn f(p0: bits[2], p1: bits[2], x: bits[32], y: bits[32],
     z: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  bit_slice.3: bits[1] = bit_slice(p1, start=0, width=1)
  sign_ext.4: bits[2] = sign_ext(bit_slice.3, new_bit_count=2)
  and.5: bits[2] = and(sign_ext.4, p0)
  bit_slice.6: bits[1] = bit_slice(p1, start=1, width=1)
  new_selector: bits[3] = concat(bit_slice.6, and.5)
  ret one_hot_sel.7: bits[32] = one_hot_sel(new_selector, cases=[x, y, z])
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/select_merging_pass.h)

## select_to_bitwise_ops - Select to Bitwise Ops {#select_to_bitwise_ops}


Converts a binary select whose two arms provably differ by a fully-known
XOR term (e.g. `sel(p, [x, xor(x, c)])`) into an XOR with an AND-masked
constant: `xor(x, and(sign_ext(p, W), c))`, with `p` complemented when the
XOR arm is the on-false case. The arms need not literally form
`xor(base, c)`: per-piece xor-with-constant differences introduced by
earlier passes (e.g. `concat_simp`) are also recognized. This is the select
pattern generated by the per-step of an unrolled CRC/shift loop.

This pass is separate from select simplification (and runs at the very end
of optimization) by design:

 * The rewrite is value-based: it only fires when the query engine can prove
   the two arms differ by a fully-known constant, unlike the rest of select
   simplification which reasons about the shape of the select itself.
 * It deliberately consumes shapes that `concat_simp` produces (wide xor
   limbs split into per-slice concats). `concat_simp` runs inside the
   fixed-point "simp" compound, and running this rewrite in the same
   fixed point would leave the two transforms repeatedly reshaping the same
   IR instead of converging.
 * It converts the select into an `and`-masked xor, which value-based
   analyses reason through less easily, so it is deferred until after those
   analyses (e.g. conditional specialization) have already run.

Runs only at optimization levels where split-based rewrites are enabled
(SplitsEnabled).

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Eligibility (`GetBinaryMuxArms`)**:
    The pass only runs when `options.splits_enabled()` is true. It inspects
    each `Select` and `PrioritySelect` with a 1-bit selector (`p`) and flat
    bit-vector type (`W >= 1`) in topological order, extracting its
    `(on_false, on_true)` arms (`cases[0]` and `cases[1]` for `Select`, or
    `default_value` and `cases[0]` for `PrioritySelect`). If either arm is
    already known to be all zeros or all ones (`IsZeroOrOnes`), the select is
    skipped so standard select simplification handles it.

2.  **Direct and Recursive XOR Delta Matching**:
    Using a `UnionQueryEngine` combining `StatelessQueryEngine` and
    `LazyTernaryQueryEngine`, the pass attempts to prove that the two arms
    differ by a fully known constant `delta` (`on_true ^ on_false == delta`):
    *   **Direct Match (`MatchXorCase`)**: Checks whether one arm is a binary
        `xor(base, c)` (or `xor(c, base)`) where `base` is the other arm and
        `c` is fully known (`query_engine.IsFullyKnown(c)`).
    *   **Recursive Structural Match (`TryFoldXorDelta`)**: Performs a
        memoized, depth-bounded (`kMaxXorFoldDepth = 1000`) structural walk
        over pairs of nodes `(a, b)` of equal bit-width:
        *   If `a == b`, the XOR delta is `0`.
        *   If both `a` and `b` are fully known constants, the delta is
            `*KnownValue(a) ^ *KnownValue(b)`.
        *   If `a` (or `b`) is a binary `xor` with a fully known operand `c`
            and variable operand `x`, recurses on `(x, b)` (or `(a, x)`) and
            XORs the resulting delta with `c`.
        *   If `a` (or `b`) is `not(x)`, recurses on `(x, b)` (or `(a, x)`)
            and bitwise-inverts the resulting delta.
        *   If both `a` and `b` are `concat` trees whose flattened operands
            (`FlattenConcats`) have pairwise matching bit-widths, recurses on
            each operand pair and concatenates the piece deltas.

3.  **Bitwise Lowering**:
    Once a `base` arm and a non-zero `delta` (`Bits`) are determined (with
    condition `cond = p` if `base == on_false`, or `cond = not(p)` if
    `base == on_true`):
    *   For 1-bit selects (`W == 1`), `delta` is `1` (`on_true ==
        not(on_false)`), and the pass avoids `sign_ext`/`and` by emitting
        `xor(on_false, p)` directly (or `not(xor(on_true, p))` when
        `on_false` is the `not`/`xor` node and `on_true` is the simpler
        base).
    *   For wider selects (`W > 1`), the select is replaced with
        `xor(base, sign_ext(cond, W))` when `delta` is all-ones, or
        `xor(base, and(sign_ext(cond, W), literal(delta)))` otherwise.

Example:

```
// Original IR
fn crc_step(p: bits[1], x: bits[8]) -> bits[8] {
  poly: bits[8] = literal(value=0x07)
  x_xor_poly: bits[8] = xor(x, poly)
  ret sel.1: bits[8] = sel(p, cases=[x, x_xor_poly])
}

// Optimized IR
fn crc_step(p: bits[1], x: bits[8]) -> bits[8] {
  mask: bits[8] = sign_ext(p, new_bit_count=8)
  delta: bits[8] = literal(value=0x07)
  masked_delta: bits[8] = and(mask, delta)
  ret xor.2: bits[8] = xor(x, masked_delta)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/select_to_bitwise_ops_pass.h)
